content:
There is no single best supplement for everyone with arthritis. Osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis are different conditions, and a result from one group of patients does not establish a benefit for another. A supplement that helps symptoms is not necessarily changing the disease or repairing a joint.

Quick answer: No supplement is best for every type of arthritis. Evidence differs by product and condition. A November 2026 Cochrane review found turmeric may make little or no difference to knee osteoarthritis pain, function or quality of life, with low certainty. NICE says not to offer glucosamine for osteoarthritis. Supplements do not replace prescribed treatment. Check safety with a pharmacist or your team.

What does NICE say about arthritis supplements?

NICE NG226, recommendations 1.4.6 and 1.4.7, says not to offer glucosamine for osteoarthritis and to explain that there is no strong evidence of benefit. This specific recommendation should not be presented as a NICE recommendation against every supplement.

For rheumatoid arthritis, NICE NG100, recommendations 1.8.9 and 1.8.10, says some complementary therapies may provide short-term symptom benefit, but there is little or no evidence for their long-term effectiveness. They should not replace conventional treatment. NICE does not provide a ranked shopping list of arthritis supplements.

Can omega-3 fish oil help rheumatoid arthritis?

Some research suggests that omega-3 may help rheumatoid arthritis symptoms, including pain, but results and study quality vary. The evidence does not mean that fish oil can replace disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs). Prescribed rheumatoid arthritis treatment can slow joint damage; do not reduce or stop it because you are trying a supplement.

Ask a pharmacist or your rheumatology team before taking fish oil, particularly if you use medicines that affect blood clotting or have a fish or shellfish allergy. Study doses are not a personal dosing recommendation. Fish oil, cod liver oil and prescription omega-3 medicines are not interchangeable. Cod liver oil also contains vitamins A and D, which can be harmful in excessive amounts.

Does turmeric or curcumin help osteoarthritis?

A Cochrane review published on 19 November 2026 found low-certainty evidence that turmeric supplements may make little or no difference to knee osteoarthritis pain, function or quality of life compared with placebo. It was very uncertain about harms. Earlier pooled reviews were more positive, but products, study selection and trustworthiness checks differ. This does not establish a benefit for other joints or types of arthritis.

Do not choose added piperine or an enhanced-absorption product simply because it promises better absorption. Piperine is an ingredient from black pepper. Increasing curcumin absorption can change safety as well as exposure. Concentrated supplements are not the same as using turmeric as a cooking spice.

Rare liver injury has been reported with turmeric and curcumin supplements. The UK Committee on Toxicity identifies a link with liver toxicity and notes that unpredictable reactions can occur. Welsh Medicines Advice Service advises avoiding medicinal turmeric or curcumin in people with liver disease, gallstones or bile-duct problems. Check any medicines and health conditions with a pharmacist before taking it. Turmeric supplements may be unsafe during pregnancy; do not assume that a food ingredient is safe at supplement doses.

Stop a turmeric or curcumin supplement and get prompt medical advice if you develop yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, loss of appetite or unexplained nausea or tiredness. Tell the clinician exactly what you have taken. Do not stop prescribed arthritis medicines on your own.

What does the research say about collagen?

A 2024 systematic review of collagen derivatives included 35 randomised trials involving 3,165 people with osteoarthritis. Its abstract reports small-to-moderate improvements in pain and function compared with controls, with moderate-certainty evidence for pain and high-certainty evidence for function. The main analysis of the primary outcome used 25 trials, rather than all 35.

That evidence should not be dismissed as no evidence, but it also does not prove that every collagen powder works, that an individual will benefit, or that supplements regrow cartilage. The review combined different collagen derivatives. Its full text was not available for this update, so this summary is limited to the published abstract. The review found no increase in adverse events or withdrawals compared with controls, but that does not establish that every product is safe for everyone. Discuss the particular product, ingredients, source and allergy risks with a pharmacist rather than treating all collagen products as equivalent.

Should you take glucosamine or chondroitin?

NICE's current osteoarthritis recommendation specifically says not to offer glucosamine because there is no strong evidence of benefit. Do not turn a conversation about dose into an endorsement to try it. Chondroitin is a separate ingredient, although products often combine the two. The local NHS patient leaflet cited below describes very little evidence that either reduces joint pain.

Glucosamine is not suitable for everyone. NHS patient information advises people taking warfarin or with seafood allergies not to take it. Ask a pharmacist before buying or continuing a product, and check combination-product labels. A supplement being available without a prescription does not establish that it is safe with your medicines.

Is vitamin D an arthritis treatment?

Vitamin D supports bone and muscle health, but it is not a replacement for arthritis treatment. NHS advice is that adults should consider a daily supplement containing 10 micrograms during autumn and winter. People with little sun exposure, including those who are frail or housebound, may need this throughout the year. People with dark skin should also consider a daily supplement throughout the year.

Check the total from all products you take, including multivitamins and cod liver oil. The NHS says not to take more than 100 micrograms a day as an adult unless your doctor has advised a different amount. Some medical conditions need individual advice. Treatment for a diagnosed deficiency may use a different dose under medical supervision.

What about ginger supplements?

Ginger supplements might help knee osteoarthritis symptoms, but much of the research is poor quality. Laboratory findings about anti-inflammatory ingredients do not establish how much benefit a person will get. Ginger can cause heartburn, stomach discomfort or diarrhoea, and herbal products can interact with medicines. Ask a pharmacist first rather than assuming that natural means harmless.

How can you check product quality without being misled?

Food supplements are not tested or regulated in the same way as licensed medicines. A high price, a familiar brand, an online review or a manufacturing certificate does not prove that a product treats arthritis.

The Traditional Herbal Registration (THR) scheme applies to traditional herbal medicines, not to every food supplement. It requires quality, safety and traditional-use evidence. A THR mark is not proof from clinical trials that a product works for arthritis. Do not confuse a manufacturing claim such as GMP with evidence of benefit or freedom from interactions.

Use a registered pharmacy for advice, check the full ingredient list and avoid products promising a cure or claiming to replace prescribed medicines. Bring the bottle, packaging or a clear photograph to your appointment. This guide does not endorse particular brands, sellers or prices.

What should you discuss before trying a supplement?

  • Which type of arthritis do you have, and what symptom are you hoping to change?
  • Could the product interact with your prescribed medicines, other supplements or health conditions?
  • Does it contain ingredients you are allergic to, or duplicate vitamins in another product?
  • What would count as a worthwhile benefit, when should it be reviewed, and what symptoms mean you should stop and seek advice?

There is no universal two-week or twelve-week trial that suits all supplements. Agree a product-specific plan with your pharmacist or treating clinician. Keep a short note of the product, start date, symptoms and any side effects. Arthritis symptoms fluctuate, so improvement after starting a product does not by itself prove that the product caused it.

When do symptoms need urgent medical help?

A suddenly very painful, hot or swollen joint, especially if it is difficult to move or put weight on, needs urgent assessment. Seek an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 advice. Joint infection can occur without a fever. Do not wait to see whether a supplement helps.

Call 999 for severe breathing difficulty, collapse or chest pain that could be a heart attack. For suspected serious supplement reactions, get medical help and tell the clinician what you took. A pharmacist or clinician can also help you report a suspected reaction through the MHRA Yellow Card scheme.

Where can you read more?

Read our turmeric and methotrexate guide, rheumatoid arthritis diet guide and diet and daily living hub. Related guides are educational information, not personal prescribing advice. Use the source list below to check the guidance behind this page.

Frequently asked questions

Can supplements replace rheumatoid arthritis medicines?

No. Do not reduce or stop prescribed treatment to try a supplement. Ask your rheumatology team or pharmacist about any product you are considering. NICE says complementary approaches should not replace conventional treatment.

Does NICE recommend glucosamine for osteoarthritis?

No. NICE NG226 says not to offer glucosamine to manage osteoarthritis because there is no strong evidence of benefit. That specific recommendation is not a blanket statement about every supplement.

Is turmeric with black pepper automatically a better choice?

No. Piperine can increase curcumin absorption, which can also affect safety. Rare liver injury has been reported with turmeric and curcumin supplements. Check the product and your medicines with a pharmacist before taking it.

Does a THR mark prove that a supplement treats arthritis?

No. THR applies to traditional herbal medicines and concerns quality, safety and evidence of traditional use. It is not a universal food-supplement mark or proof from clinical trials of arthritis effectiveness.

key_takeaways: No supplement is best for every type of arthritis or replaces prescribed treatment.
NICE says not to offer glucosamine for osteoarthritis; do not extend that statement to every supplement.
Curcumin products have differing evidence and safety. Enhanced absorption is not automatically safer or better.
Ask a pharmacist about medicines, allergies, product ingredients and a plan for review before starting a supplement.
